title: UFC vs boxing marketing: promote personas, not events, and control the distribution
summary: Ross Jenkins compares UFC's centralized, fighter-persona-driven, digital-first model with boxing's fragmented promoter model and print/PPV reach. He draws marketing and business lessons on brand control, storytelling, fair pay for brand reputation, and using digital channels for younger audiences.

principles.text: Promote the people and their stories, not just the events; personas draw audiences in.
principles.quote: Instead of focusing on the events themselves, UFC tends to promote the fighters by building up their personas and their stories. It’s an effective tool that can draw more people in.

principles.text: Owning the whole value chain gives you control and higher margins, but can strain the people you rely on.
principles.quote: Looking at the operating side, UFC as a whole earns more since everything is produced in-house. However, the same can’t be said of their fighters.

principles.text: Match channel to audience: traditional audiences respond to print and live, younger adults to digital.
principles.quote: Boxing is concentrated on folks who are more traditional; that’s why they focus their promoting strategies using traditional marketing. On the other hand, UFC garners more viewership from younger adults.

principles.text: Ethical treatment of partners is a brand asset; buyers drop products with questionable sourcing.
principles.quote: If a product they like wasn’t sourced ethically, then they’ll drop it even if they like it.

principles.text: Don't restrict partners' outside deals; blocking sponsorships can cost you ad-revenue opportunities.
principles.quote: They should also be allowed more sponsorships and deals. Restricting these can end up costing them fewer opportunities from ad revenues.

principles.text: Even a solid strategy should fully use social and digital marketing tools to leverage growth.
principles.quote: Utilizing every aspect of digital marketing will help UFC leverage the sport.
